rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes shared memory size from 256 to 257 floats. With block_size=256 (fixed constant), tid=threadIdx.x ranges [0,255]. All shared memory accesses are: (1) shared_mem[tid] for writes, accessing indices 0-255; (2) shared_mem[tid+stride] in reduction where max(tid+stride) = 127+128 = 255. Index 256 is never accessed. For input shape [128,1], size=128, num_blocks=1. The extra allocated element at index 256 is dead memory.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation only increases the shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 floats, adding one unused element at index 256. The kernel's block_size is hardcoded to 256, meaning threadIdx.x always ranges from 0 to 255. All shared memory reads and writes use tid (0-255) or tid+stride where the maximum possible index is 255 (when tid=127 and stride=128 in the first reduction iteration). With the fixed input shape of [128,1], only 128 elements are processed by a single block, and threads 128-255 simply contribute 0.0f to the reduction. Since index 256 is never read or written, the mutation is functionally identical to the original regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable. The mutation allocates unused shared memory (index 256) that is never accessed by any thread under the fixed block_size=256 configuration. No input values can change the memory access pattern since it depends solely on thread indices and block dimensions, not on data values.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should recognize that increasing array allocations beyond the maximum accessed index produces equivalent mutants. A static analysis rule could detect when array size increases don't affect any reachable array access patterns based on fixed launch parameters.
